children: By Jesse Newman
Organic children's food company Once Upon a Farm is learning how quickly a recall can change a company's fortunes.

The buzzy food company, which made its debut on the New York Stock Exchange in February, voluntarily recalled one of its signature products — soft-baked bars called Tractor Wheels — following reports that they pose a potential choking hazard. It has also fielded separate concerns from parents who found what looked to be pieces of metal in the company's products.
Now the stock has taken a hit, plunging 38% last week and wiping out $242 million of market value. Tractor Wheels bars made up about 18% of Once Upon a Farm's sales this year.

Once Upon a Farm, co-founded by John Foraker, a veteran food executive, and actress Jennifer Garner, caters to millennial and Gen Z parents with pouches, oat bars, frozen meals and pantry snacks made without added sugar, preservatives or artificial ingredients. The company has pitched itself as a pioneer in childhood nutrition, with a connection to consumers built on trust, quality and transparency.

The recall follows reports that the Tractor Wheels bars can quickly form into a dense, dry and sticky mass during consumption, according to the company's announcement on the U.S. Food and Drug Administration's website. Once Upon a Farm said the issue can be a hazard for toddlers. It said that no injuries had been reported.
"Consumer safety is our number one thing and we don't mess around with it," Foraker, the company's chief executive, said.

Foraker said Once Upon a Farm is aware of three reports of choking incidents tied to Tractor Wheels. The company began investigating the issue immediately and opted to recall all of its Tractor Wheels products when it couldn't quickly isolate the problem to a particular batch, Foraker said.

Earlier this year, some parents began offering other safety warnings about Once Upon a Farm's snacks in social-media posts. Melanie Delgado, an Ohio mother of two young girls, said she found two sharp pieces of metal in a Tractor Wheel that she was feeding to her one-year-old daughter in August.
"I was so distraught," Delgado said, adding that she had originally packed the snack in her 5-year-old's lunch bag several days prior.
Delgado contacted Once Upon a Farm, which asked her to mail the material back so that it could investigate, according to emails viewed by The Wall Street Journal.

The company told Delgado that it had traced the material to the laminated foil bags in which some of its ingredients arrive. One message said that, along with an independent food-safety consultant, Once Upon a Farm had determined that the material didn't pose a health or safety risk, but that the quality failure was still unacceptable.

"We failed you and our promise, and that is not something we're willing to accept," the company said in an email. "You shouldn't have had to feel that jolt of fear, and we are very sorry that you did."
Once Upon a Farm also detailed some of the changes it had made involving its bags to help eliminate the risk that the material could wind up in its products.

Foraker said that the foreign material wasn't metal, and that the issue had been fixed. "In food manufacturing, there are issues that arise from time to time," Foraker said. "You just have to work through them."

Other parents have complained on social media about finding bits of blue plastic in Once Upon a Farm's bars. A spokeswoman for the company said that it had promptly investigated the complaints earlier this year, identified the root cause and immediately resolved it. No injuries were reported, the spokeswoman said.

Foraker, who previously led Annie's Homegrown, said he has learned from previous recalls, including one not long after Annie's 2012 IPO. That recall involved a new line of frozen pizzas, which the company recalled because of the possible presence of metal-mesh fragments caused by a faulty screen at a third-party flour mill.

Annie's emerged from that recall more trusted by consumers, Foraker said, adding that Once Upon a Farm is now doing everything it can to make sure consumers can trust it to bring its toddler snacks back to market.
Delgado said she has bought Once Upon a Farm's products for years because she felt that she could trust the brand, and its ingredients. "I haven't purchased anything from them since," she said.
